--- title: "Reshaping" subtitle: "≈ `pivot_longer()` · `pivot_wider()` · `separate_*()` · `unite()` · `complete()`" jupyter: python3 --- Reshaping moves values between positions (column name, row, cell) without changing them. tidyr and Polars have the same operations under different names. They differ in what happens when the data doesn't fit: mixed dtypes, duplicate cells, a wrong number of pieces, and row order. This chapter covers the verbs, then those cases. ## In tidyverse {#sec-rs-tidyverse} R4DS's three rules of tidy data: each variable is a column, each observation is a row, each value is a cell. The tidyr verbs move data into those positions: ```r library(tidyr) who2 |> # lengthen; names hold three variables pivot_longer(!(country:year), names_to = c("diagnosis", "gender", "age"), names_sep = "_", values_to = "count", values_drop_na = TRUE) household |> # two value columns per child: .value pivot_longer(!family, names_to = c(".value", "child"), names_sep = "_", values_drop_na = TRUE) weather |> # widen: one column per origin pivot_wider(id_cols = time_hour, names_from = origin, values_from = temp) penguins |> # make implicit missing rows explicit count(species, island) |> complete(species, island, fill = list(n = 0)) ``` Polars splits the same work across `unpivot()`, `pivot()`, string methods, `explode()` / `unnest()`, and joins. ## Mental model {#sec-rs-model} ```text index on index variable value ┌─────┬────┐ ┌───────┬───────┐ ┌─────┬────┐ ┌───────┐ ┌───────┐ WIDE │ EWR │ 1 │ │ 39.02 │ 26.06 │ unpivot │ EWR │ 1 │ │ temp │ │ 39.02 │ LONG │ JFK │ 1 │ │ 39.02 │ 26.06 │ ───────► │ JFK │ 1 │ │ temp │ │ 39.02 │ └─────┴────┘ └───────┴───────┘ │ EWR │ 1 │ │ dewp │ │ 26.06 │ origin hour temp dewp │ JFK │ 1 │ │ dewp │ │ 26.06 │ └─────┴────┘ └───────┘ └───────┘ ◄─────── pivot(on="variable", index=["origin", "hour"], values="value") unpivot: all `on` columns feed ONE value column → their dtypes must unify pivot = group_by(index, on).agg(f(values)), then each distinct `on` value becomes a column → f must give one value per cell ``` Two consequences. `unpivot()` needs a common dtype for the columns it stacks (@sec-rs-supertype). `pivot()` is an aggregation, so duplicate `(index, on)` pairs need an aggregate function (@sec-rs-duplicates). | tidyr argument | Polars argument | Note | |---|---|---| | `pivot_longer(cols)` | `unpivot(on=)` | `on=None` = every column not in `index` | | (implicit: all other columns) | `unpivot(index=)` | **not** implicit: omit it and those columns are dropped | | `names_to` / `values_to` | `variable_name=` / `value_name=` | defaults `"variable"` / `"value"` | | `names_sep` / `names_pattern` | `.str.split_exact()` / `.str.extract_groups()` + `unnest()` | a separate step (@sec-rs-names) | | `values_drop_na = TRUE` | `.drop_nulls("value")` | | | `id_cols` / `names_from` / `values_from` | `index=` / `on=` / `values=` | | | `values_fn` | `aggregate_function=` | default: one value per cell, else error | | `values_fill` | `.fill_null()` afterwards | also fills nulls from the data (@sec-rs-empty-cells) | | `names_sort = TRUE` | `sort_columns=True` | | | `names_sep` (wider) | `separator=` | used only with several `values` | : Argument names {.striped} One-line translations are in the cheatsheet's [Reshape](../overview/polars-cheatsheet.qmd#sec-cs-reshape) section. ## Mechanics {#sec-rs-mechanics} ::: {#1415acf3 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import datetime as dt import polars as pl import polars.selectors as cs from pl_notes import datasets penguins_df = datasets.penguins() weather_df = datasets.weather() weather_df_jan1 = weather_df.filter( pl.col("month") == 1, pl.col("day") == 1, pl.col("hour").is_in([1, 2]) ).select("origin", "hour", "temp", "dewp", "humid") weather_df_jan1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

originhourtempdewphumid

"EWR"139.0226.0659.37
"EWR"239.0226.9661.63
"JFK"139.0226.0659.37
"JFK"239.0226.0659.37
"LGA"139.9226.0657.33
"LGA"241.026.0654.97
``` ::: ::: ### Lengthening: `unpivot()` {#sec-rs-unpivot} ::: {#a7b6fb8b .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} weather_df_jan1.unpivot( ["temp", "dewp", "humid"], index=["origin", "hour"], variable_name="measure", value_name="value", ).sort("origin", "hour", "measure").head(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
shape: (4, 4)
originhourmeasurevalue
stri64strf64
"EWR"1"dewp"26.06
"EWR"1"humid"59.37
"EWR"1"temp"39.02
"EWR"2"dewp"26.96
``` ::: ::: `on` takes names or a selector. Without `index`, every column not in `on` is **dropped**, where `pivot_longer()` would keep it as an identifier: ::: {#43aa2db0 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} { "index given": weather_df_jan1.unpivot(cs.float(), index=["origin", "hour"]).columns, "index omitted": weather_df_jan1.unpivot(cs.float()).columns, } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` {'index given': ['origin', 'hour', 'variable', 'value'], 'index omitted': ['variable', 'value']} ``` ::: ::: (`melt()`, the old name, no longer exists in 2.0.) **Row order is unspecified**: the docstring says so, and it changes with the engine. Eager `unpivot()` stacks column by column; the same query run lazily came out row by row here, which is `pivot_longer()`'s order: ::: {#fab10b9d .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} tiny_df = pl.DataFrame({"id": ["a", "b", "c"], "x1": [1, 2, 3], "x2": [4, 5, 6]}) { "eager": tiny_df.unpivot(index="id")["id"].to_list(), "lazy": tiny_df.lazy().unpivot(index="id").collect()["id"].to_list(), } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` {'eager': ['a', 'b', 'c', 'a', 'b', 'c'], 'lazy': ['a', 'a', 'b', 'b', 'c', 'c']} ``` ::: ::: On a large lazy frame the rows come in interleaved chunks. If order matters, `.sort()` by the index and variable columns. ### Names that carry data {#sec-rs-names} `pivot_longer()` splits names during the pivot. `unpivot()` doesn't; split the `variable` column afterwards. A small `who2`-style frame: ::: {#228baa74 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} who_df = pl.DataFrame({ "country": ["Thailand", "Thailand", "Laos"], "year": [2012, 2013, 2013], "sp_m_014": [120, 98, 15], "sp_f_1524": [310, 287, 40], "rel_m_65": [None, 12, 3], }) ( who_df.unpivot(index=["country", "year"], variable_name="key", value_name="count") .with_columns( pl.col("key").str.split_exact("_", 2) # 2 splits → struct of 3 fields .struct.rename_fields(["diagnosis", "gender", "age"]) ) .unnest("key") # struct fields → columns .drop_nulls("count") # values_drop_na = TRUE .sort("country", "year", "diagnosis", "gender") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
shape: (8, 6)
countryyeardiagnosisgenderagecount
stri64strstrstri64
"Laos"2013"rel""m""65"3
"Laos"2013"sp""f""1524"40
"Laos"2013"sp""m""014"15
"Thailand"2012"sp""f""1524"310
"Thailand"2012"sp""m""014"120
"Thailand"2013"rel""m""65"12
"Thailand"2013"sp""f""1524"287
"Thailand"2013"sp""m""014"98
``` ::: ::: `split_exact(by, n)` counts **splits**, not pieces, and names the fields `field_0`, `field_1`, …, hence `rename_fields()`. For `names_pattern`, use `str.extract_groups()`: named capture groups such as `(?[mf])` become the field names, so no rename is needed (see the recipe in @sec-rs-recipes). ```text "sp_m_014" ──str.split("_")──────────► ["sp", "m", "014"] List any length → explode() ──str.split_exact("_", 2)─► {"sp", "m", "014"} Struct fixed fields → unnest() ──str.extract_groups(re)──► {diagnosis: "sp", …} Struct named fields → unnest() ``` ### Several value columns: `.value` {#sec-rs-value} `.value` in `names_to` means "this part of the name is a column name, not data". Polars has no sentinel. A `household`-style frame, two columns per child: ::: {#979a4fe3 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} household_df = pl.DataFrame({ "family": [1, 2, 3], "dob_child1": [dt.date(1998, 11, 26), dt.date(1996, 6, 22), dt.date(2002, 7, 11)], "dob_child2": [dt.date(2000, 1, 29), None, dt.date(2004, 4, 5)], "name_child1": ["Malee", "Somchai", "Nok"], "name_child2": ["Anan", None, "Ploy"], }) ``` ::: **Route 1: unpivot, split, pivot the `.value` part back out.** ::: {#ff2f605f .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( household_df.unpivot(index="family") .with_columns(pl.col("variable").str.split_exact("_", 1).struct.rename_fields([".value", "child"])) .unnest("variable") .pivot(".value", index=["family", "child"], values="value") .drop_nulls() .sort("family", "child") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}
shape: (5, 4)
familychilddobname
i64strstrstr
1"child1""1998-11-26""Malee"
1"child2""2000-01-29""Anan"
2"child1""1996-06-22""Somchai"
3"child1""2002-07-11""Nok"
3"child2""2004-04-05""Ploy"
``` ::: ::: It works, but `dob` comes back as `str`: Date and String had to share one value column on the way (@sec-rs-supertype). **Route 2: stack the column groups.** One `select()` per child, then `pl.concat()`. Every column keeps its dtype: ::: {#69147eb7 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.concat([ household_df.select("family", child=pl.lit(c), dob=f"dob_{c}", name=f"name_{c}") for c in ["child1", "child2"] ]).drop_nulls().sort("family", "child") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ```{=html}
shape: (5, 4)
familychilddobname
i64strdatestr
1"child1"1998-11-26"Malee"
1"child2"2000-01-29"Anan"
2"child1"1996-06-22"Somchai"
3"child1"2002-07-11"Nok"
3"child2"2004-04-05"Ploy"
``` ::: ::: ### Widening: `pivot()` {#sec-rs-pivot} ::: {#5fe9c4e8 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} weather_df_wide = weather_df.pivot("origin", index="time_hour", values="temp") weather_df_wide.head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}
shape: (3, 4)
time_hourEWRJFKLGA
datetime[μs, America/New_York]f64f64f64
2013-01-01 01:00:00 EST39.0239.0239.92
2013-01-01 02:00:00 EST39.0239.0241.0
2013-01-01 03:00:00 EST39.0239.9241.0
``` ::: ::: **Columns** follow the first appearance of each `on` value, like `pivot_wider()`; `sort_columns=True` sorts them and `on_columns=` picks and orders them. **Rows** follow the first appearance of each `index` value (eager `maintain_order=True`). That is not chronological here: `weather` is sorted by origin, so hours that EWR lacks first appear in the JFK and LGA blocks and land at the bottom: ::: {#4d03ea37 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} weather_df_wide["time_hour"].is_sorted(), weather_df_wide.tail(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ``` (False, shape: (2, 4) ┌────────────────────────────────┬──────┬──────┬───────┐ │ time_hour ┆ EWR ┆ JFK ┆ LGA │ │ --- ┆ --- ┆ --- ┆ --- │ │ datetime[μs, America/New_York] ┆ f64 ┆ f64 ┆ f64 │ ╞════════════════════════════════╪══════╪══════╪═══════╡ │ 2013-01-01 12:00:00 EST ┆ null ┆ null ┆ 37.94 │ │ 2013-08-22 18:00:00 EDT ┆ null ┆ null ┆ 75.92 │ └────────────────────────────────┴──────┴──────┴───────┘) ``` ::: ::: With several `values`, names are `{value}{separator}{on}`, as in tidyr: ::: {#3c87bee7 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} weather_df.pivot("origin", index="time_hour", values=["temp", "dewp"]).columns ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ``` ['time_hour', 'temp_EWR', 'temp_JFK', 'temp_LGA', 'dewp_EWR', 'dewp_JFK', 'dewp_LGA'] ``` ::: ::: Non-string `on` values are converted to names (`2007` → `"2007"`, null → `"null"`). Several `on` columns, e.g. `on=["sex", "year"]`, give struct-literal names such as `{"male",2007}` instead of tidyr's `male_2007`. Build one key with `pl.concat_str("sex", "year", separator="_")` and pivot on that. ### Aggregating cells {#sec-rs-agg} The mental model said `pivot()` is `group_by().agg()` plus a spread. Proof: ::: {#2edb6e74 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} pivot_direct = penguins_df.pivot( "island", index="species", values="body_mass_g", aggregate_function="mean", sort_columns=True ).sort("species") pivot_two_step = ( penguins_df.group_by("species", "island").agg(pl.col("body_mass_g").mean()) .pivot("island", index="species", values="body_mass_g", sort_columns=True) .sort("species") ) pivot_two_step.equals(pivot_direct) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ``` True ``` ::: ::: `aggregate_function` takes `"min"`, `"max"`, `"first"`, `"last"`, `"sum"`, `"mean"`, `"median"`, `"len"`, or an expression on `pl.element()` (the values in one cell). The default, `None`, means `"item"`: exactly one value per cell, or a `ComputeError` (@sec-rs-duplicates). tidyr's list-column output is `implode()`: ::: {#790d36de .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins_df.pivot( "island", index="species", values="year", aggregate_function=pl.element().unique().sort().implode(), sort_columns=True, ).sort("species") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ```{=html}
shape: (3, 4)
speciesBiscoeDreamTorgersen
strlist[i64]list[i64]list[i64]
"Adelie"[2007, 2008, 2009][2007, 2008, 2009][2007, 2008, 2009]
"Chinstrap"[][2007, 2008, 2009][]
"Gentoo"[2007, 2008, 2009][][]
``` ::: ::: Cells with no rows hold `[]`, the aggregate of nothing (@sec-rs-empty-cells). ### Lazy `pivot()` needs `on_columns=` {#sec-rs-lazy-pivot} A `LazyFrame` knows its output schema before it reads data ([Data Model](../core/data-model.qmd#sec-dm-containers)). A pivot's schema depends on the distinct `on` values, so lazy `pivot()` makes you list them: ::: {#e1f21cf1 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} weather_df.lazy().pivot("origin", index="time_hour", values="temp") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
TypeError: LazyFrame.pivot() missing 1 required positional argument: 'on_columns'
``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {#4fb3ec30 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} origins = weather_df["origin"].unique().sort() # the data pass, done eagerly weather_df.lazy().pivot( "origin", on_columns=origins, index="time_hour", values="temp" ).collect_schema() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ``` Schema([('time_hour', Datetime(time_unit='us', time_zone='America/New_York')), ('EWR', Float64), ('JFK', Float64), ('LGA', Float64)]) ``` ::: ::: `on_columns` filters as well as lists: an unlisted value is dropped silently, and a listed value with no data becomes an all-null column. ::: {#41fd3fb0 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} weather_df.lazy().pivot( "origin", on_columns=["EWR", "JFK", "BOS"], index="time_hour", values="temp" ).sort("time_hour").collect().head(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ```{=html}
shape: (2, 4)
time_hourEWRJFKBOS
datetime[μs, America/New_York]f64f64f64
2013-01-01 01:00:00 EST39.0239.02null
2013-01-01 02:00:00 EST39.0239.02null
``` ::: ::: LGA is gone, BOS is empty, nothing warned. Lazy `pivot()` also defaults to `maintain_order=False`, so its row order changes between runs; sort it. dbplyr's `pivot_wider()` faces the same problem and runs an extra query to find the names; Polars makes that step yours. ### Lists and structs: `explode()` and `unnest()` {#sec-rs-nested} `explode()` ≈ `unnest_longer()`: one row per list element. Null and empty lists are treated differently: ::: {#ce7a0cb4 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} orders_df = pl.DataFrame({"order": [1, 2, 3, 4], "items": [["tea", "milk"], [], None, ["rice"]]}) { "default": orders_df.explode("items")["order"].to_list(), "keep_nulls=False": orders_df.explode("items", keep_nulls=False)["order"].to_list(), "empty_as_null=True": orders_df.explode("items", empty_as_null=True)["order"].to_list(), } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=18} ``` {'default': [1, 1, 3, 4], 'keep_nulls=False': [1, 1, 4], 'empty_as_null=True': [1, 1, 2, 3, 4]} ``` ::: ::: By default the empty order 2 disappears and the null order 3 stays as a null row. `unnest_longer()`'s default (`keep_empty = FALSE`) drops both, which is `keep_nulls=False`; `keep_empty = TRUE` keeps both, which is `empty_as_null=True`. Exploding several columns at once requires equal list lengths in every row, otherwise `ShapeError`. `unnest()` ≈ `unnest_wider()`, for **struct** columns. `separator=` prefixes the field names, like `names_sep`: ::: {#1634ba1c .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins_df.head(2).select( "species", bill=pl.struct(length="bill_length_mm", depth="bill_depth_mm") ).unnest("bill", separator="_") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=19} ```{=html}
shape: (2, 3)
speciesbill_lengthbill_depth
strf64f64
"Adelie"39.118.7
"Adelie"39.517.4
``` ::: ::: A list column must become a struct first: `.list.to_struct(fields=[...])` (short lists pad with null), or take elements with `.list.get(i, null_on_oob=True)`. ### Splitting and uniting strings {#sec-rs-strings} The three splitters differ in what they return and in how they treat a wrong number of pieces: ::: {#fdc916a7 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} codes_df = pl.DataFrame({"key": ["sp_m_014", "ep_m", "sp_f_25_34"]}) codes_df.with_columns( split=pl.col("key").str.split("_"), # List: all pieces split_exact=pl.col("key").str.split_exact("_", 2), # Struct: exactly 3 fields splitn=pl.col("key").str.splitn("_", 3), # Struct: at most 3, rest in the last ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ```{=html}
shape: (3, 4)
keysplitsplit_exactsplitn
strlist[str]struct[3]struct[3]
"sp_m_014"["sp", "m", "014"]{"sp","m","014"}{"sp","m","014"}
"ep_m"["ep", "m"]{"ep","m",null}{"ep","m",null}
"sp_f_25_34"["sp", "f", … "34"]{"sp","f","25"}{"sp","f","25_34"}
``` ::: ::: | tidyr | Polars | Too few pieces | Too many pieces | |---|---|---|---| | `separate_longer_delim()` | `str.split()` + `explode()` | n/a | n/a | | `separate_wider_delim()` | `str.split_exact()` + `unnest()` | null-padded | **dropped** | | `separate_wider_delim(too_many = "merge")` | `str.splitn()` + `unnest()` | null-padded | kept in the last field | | `separate_wider_regex()` | `str.extract_groups()` + `unnest()` | no match → all null | no match → all null | : tidyr errors on a wrong piece count by default; Polars never does {.striped} `str.split(by, literal=False)` splits on a regex. `unite()` ≈ `pl.concat_str()`. Non-string columns are cast for you; nulls are not. `unite()` writes the text `"NA"`; `concat_str()` makes the whole result null unless `ignore_nulls=True` (≈ `na.rm = TRUE`): ::: {#4d75fafd .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} parts_df = pl.DataFrame({"diagnosis": ["sp", "rel", None], "gender": ["m", None, "f"], "age": [14, 65, 25]}) parts_df.with_columns( key=pl.concat_str("diagnosis", "gender", "age", separator="_"), key_skip=pl.concat_str("diagnosis", "gender", "age", separator="_", ignore_nulls=True), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=21} ```{=html}
shape: (3, 5)
diagnosisgenderagekeykey_skip
strstri64strstr
"sp""m"14"sp_m_14""sp_m_14"
"rel"null65null"rel_65"
null"f"25null"f_25"
``` ::: ::: `unite()` also drops its inputs (`remove = TRUE`); in Polars, `.drop()` them. ### `transpose()` {#sec-rs-transpose} `t()` for frames. Pass `include_header=True` to keep the old column names, and `column_names=` to take the new ones from a column. Each new column needs one dtype, so mixed-type rows come out as `str`; for anything but display, unpivot + pivot keeps dtypes under control. ::: {#8aebc6b1 .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins_df.group_by("species").agg(cs.ends_with("_mm").mean().round(1)).sort("species").transpose( include_header=True, header_name="measure", column_names="species" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=22} ```{=html}
shape: (3, 4)
measureAdelieChinstrapGentoo
strf64f64f64
"bill_length_mm"38.848.847.5
"bill_depth_mm"18.318.415.0
"flipper_length_mm"190.0195.8217.2
``` ::: ::: ### Making implicit missing rows explicit: `complete()` {#sec-rs-complete} A row that doesn't exist is an *implicit* missing value ([Missing Values](../types/missing.qmd)). `complete()` is a cross join of the unique values, then a left join of the data onto that grid: ::: {#72b24b0a .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguin_counts_df = penguins_df.group_by("species", "island").agg(n=pl.len()) species_islands_df = penguins_df.select("species").unique().join( penguins_df.select("island").unique(), how="cross" # expand(species, island) ) ( species_islands_df .join(penguin_counts_df, on=["species", "island"], how="left") # complete(species, island) .with_columns(pl.col("n").fill_null(0)) # fill = list(n = 0) .sort("species", "island") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=23} ```{=html}
shape: (9, 3)
speciesislandn
strstru32
"Adelie""Biscoe"44
"Adelie""Dream"56
"Adelie""Torgersen"52
"Chinstrap""Biscoe"0
"Chinstrap""Dream"68
"Chinstrap""Torgersen"0
"Gentoo""Biscoe"124
"Gentoo""Dream"0
"Gentoo""Torgersen"0
``` ::: ::: | tidyr | Polars | |---|---| | `expand(df, a, b)` | `df.select("a").unique().join(df.select("b").unique(), how="cross")` | | `expand(df, nesting(a, b))` | `df.select("a", "b").unique()` | | `crossing(a = x, b = y)` | `pl.DataFrame({"a": x}).join(pl.DataFrame({"b": y}), how="cross")` | | `complete(df, a, b)` | `grid.join(df, on=["a", "b"], how="left")` | | the missing combinations only | `grid.join(df, on=["a", "b"], how="anti")` | | `full_seq(x, 1)` in `complete()` | build the grid from `pl.int_range()` / `pl.datetime_range()` | : `complete()` and friends {.striped} Join row order is not guaranteed without `maintain_order=`; see [Joins](joins.qmd). ## Where it bites {#sec-rs-gotchas} | tidyr behaviour | Polars behaviour | |---|---| | `pivot_longer()` keeps non-`cols` columns as ids | `unpivot()` without `index` drops them | | `pivot_longer()` errors on incompatible types | `unpivot()` casts to a supertype, silently | | `pivot_longer()` output goes row by row | `unpivot()` row order is unspecified | | duplicate cells: a warning and list-columns | duplicate cells: `ComputeError` | | missing combinations are `NA`, whatever `values_fn` is | `"sum"` and `"len"` give 0, the others null | | `values_fill` fills only missing combinations | `fill_null()` also fills nulls from the data | | `names_from = c(a, b)` → `a_b` | `on=["a", "b"]` → `{"a","b"}` | | `separate_wider_*()` errors on a wrong piece count | `split_exact()` pads with null or drops pieces | | `unite()` writes `"NA"` | `concat_str()` returns null | | `unnest_longer()` drops `NULL` and empty elements | `explode()` keeps nulls, drops empty lists | : The differences at a glance {.striped} ### `unpivot()` casts to a supertype {#sec-rs-supertype} The `value` column has one dtype, so Polars casts every `on` column to their supertype, without a warning, including casts that destroy meaning: ::: {#7f7a6ce9 .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} mixed_df = pl.DataFrame({"id": [1], "n": [1], "x": [1.5], "s": ["a"], "d": [dt.date(2013, 1, 1)]}) { pair: str(mixed_df.unpivot(list(pair), index="id")["value"].to_list()) for pair in [("n", "x"), ("n", "s"), ("d", "s"), ("d", "n")] } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=24} ``` {('n', 'x'): '[1.0, 1.5]', ('n', 's'): "['1', 'a']", ('d', 's'): "['2013-01-01', 'a']", ('d', 'n'): '[15706, 1]'} ``` ::: ::: Integer + float → float is what R does too. The other three are errors in `pivot_longer()`, because vctrs won't combine character with double, or Date with integer. Polars turns the date into `"2013-01-01"` next to a string, and into `15706` (days since 1970) next to an integer. Only types with no supertype at all, such as a list and an integer, raise a `SchemaError`. **Rule:** check the `value` dtype after `unpivot()`. Unpivot same-typed columns (`on=cs.numeric()`), or use route 2 of @sec-rs-value. ### One cell, two values {#sec-rs-duplicates} Widen `weather` by origin, keyed by date and hour: ::: {#ebb06e2a .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} weather_df.pivot("origin", index=["month", "day", "hour"], values="temp") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
ComputeError: aggregation 'item' expected no or a single value, got 2 values

This error occurred in the following expression:
	col("temp").filter([(col("origin")) ==v ("EWR")]).item(allow_empty=true)
``` ::: ::: ::: `hour` is local clock time. On 3 November 2013 the clocks went back, so 01:00 happened twice. `time_hour` is an instant, so it is unique, and the earlier pivot worked: ::: {#4faa8545 .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} weather_df.filter(pl.col("month") == 11, pl.col("day") == 3, pl.col("hour") == 1).select( "origin", "hour", "temp", "time_hour" ).sort("origin", "time_hour").head(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=26} ```{=html}

Find the duplicates with a grouped count, as R4DS does: ::: {#6f4db08a .cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} weather_df.group_by("origin", "month", "day", "hour").len().filter(pl.col("len") > 1).sort("origin") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=27} ```{=html}

For `"sum"` and `"len"` that is 0: ::: {#4ce6dcca .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} { agg: penguins_df.pivot("island", index="species", values="year", aggregate_function=agg) .filter(pl.col("species") == "Gentoo").select("Dream").item() for agg in ["len", "sum", "mean", "first"] } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=28} ``` {'len': 0, 'sum': 0, 'mean': None, 'first': None} ``` ::: ::: No Gentoo lives on Dream. A count of 0 is right; a sum of 0 hides the difference between "measured zero" and "never measured". The reverse problem: `.fill_null(0)` after a pivot fills missing combinations *and* nulls that were in the data, because both are null by then. `values_fill` fills only the former. If the difference matters, pivot a `"len"` table too and use it to find the real gaps. ### `split_exact()` never complains {#sec-rs-split-silent} In @sec-rs-strings, `"ep_m"` was padded with null and `"sp_f_25_34"` lost `"34"`. `separate_wider_delim()` would have stopped. Check the piece count yourself: ::: {#36d9fd78 .cell execution_count=29} ``` {.python .cell-code} codes_df.filter(pl.col("key").str.split("_").list.len() != 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=29} ```{=html}
shape: (2, 1)
key

``` ::: ::: `extract_groups()` is the same: a non-matching string becomes all nulls. Anchor the pattern (`^…$`) and filter for the nulls. ### Lists vs structs {#sec-rs-list-struct} `str.split()` returns a List; `split_exact()`, `splitn()` and `extract_groups()` return a Struct. `explode()` takes lists and `unnest()` takes structs, so `str.split()` followed by `unnest()` fails: ::: {#97651d84 .cell execution_count=30} ``` {.python .cell-code} codes_df.with_columns(pl.col("key").str.split("_")).unnest("key") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
InvalidOperationError: invalid dtype: expected 'Struct', got 'List(String)' for 'key'
``` ::: ::: ::: `explode()` on a plain String column fails the same way: a string is not a list of characters. ## Recipes {#sec-rs-recipes} **A summary table, wide by species, for display.** Unpivot, aggregate inside `pivot()`, and fix the row order with an `Enum` (≈ `fct_inorder()`): ::: {#79c032ee .cell execution_count=31} ``` {.python .cell-code} measure_cols = ["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm", "flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g"] ( penguins_df.unpivot(measure_cols, index="species", variable_name="measure") .with_columns(pl.col("measure").cast(pl.Enum(measure_cols))) .pivot("species", index="measure", values="value", aggregate_function=pl.element().mean().round(1), sort_columns=True) .sort("measure") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=31} ```{=html}

Build every hour with `pl.datetime_range()`, cross it with the origins, and left-join the data. A `True` flag added before the join marks the rows that existed: ::: {#d7ff8c68 .cell execution_count=34} ``` {.python .cell-code} hours_df = weather_df.select( time_hour=pl.datetime_range(pl.col("time_hour").min(), pl.col("time_hour").max(), "1h") ) weather_grid_df = weather_df.select(pl.col("origin").unique()).join(hours_df, how="cross") weather_df_complete = weather_grid_df.join( weather_df.with_columns(observed=pl.lit(True)), on=["origin", "time_hour"], how="left" ) weather_df_complete.group_by("origin").agg( added_rows=pl.col("observed").is_null().sum(), null_temp=pl.col("temp").is_null().sum(), ).sort("origin") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=34} ```{=html}

The range is time-zone aware, so 3 November has both 01:00 EDT and 01:00 EST.
